CIV-NZ.summary: The N'Zi river basin, a 35,500 km² sub-basin of the Bandama in Côte d'Ivoire. The river rises near Ferkessédougou at about 400 m and flows north–south across low plateaux, from the savanna north to the forest south.
CIV-NZ.ecosystem: Savanna in the north and centre gives way to forest in the south, across plateaux of 100–400 m broken by the Baoulé range; annual rainfall rises from under 1,200 mm to over 1,600 mm southwards.
CIV-NZ.livelihoods: Smallholder farming: in inland valleys surveyed around Bouaké, households cultivate about 2.7 ha on average, with rice ranked the first crop and yam the second.
CIV-NZ.why_it_matters: Its seasonally flooded inland valleys feed farm households, with rice the top-ranked crop, but river flow has fallen far more than rainfall (deficits of 52% against 16%).

sources.note: Simulations croisées / relation pluie-débit, N'zi-Bandama (Kouassi et al., Comptes Rendus Géoscience 344(5), 2012, open access) §2 Présentation de la zone d'étude: sub-basin of the Bandama; 35 500 km2; 3°49'-5°22' W, 6°00'-9°26' N; source in the Ferkessédougou region at 400 m; flows north-south; low-relief plateaux; savanna centre/north, forest south.

Variabilité climatique, bassin du N'zi (Kouassi et al., Cybergeo doc. 513, 2010, CC BY 4.0) §3: same 35 500 km2 and coordinates; basin runs from the savanna region in the north to the forest zone in the south.

Kouassi et al. 2012 §2: plateaux 100-400 m on average, monotony broken by the chaîne Baoulé; savanna vegetation in centre and north, forest in south; rainfall <1200 mm north, 1200-1600 mm centre, >1600 mm south.
Kouassi et al. 2010 §4-6: three regimes; mean annual rainfall 1951-2000 below 1200 mm north of ~8°N, 1200-1600 mm in the centre, above 1600 mm south of ~7°N.

Farming systems, food security and ecosystem services in inland valleys (Alemayehu et al., Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 6:892818, 2022, CC BY 4.0; doi 10.3389/fsufs.2022.892818) Table 3, Bouaké column (n = 226 households, 8 inland valleys): land cultivated 2.7 ± 3.8 ha; farmers growing rice 59%; use of IV bottom 68%. Results 'Main crops': rice ranked first in all regions, yam second in Bouaké. SUB-AREA: Bouaké survey region only (approx. 7°38'-7°57' N, 4°44'-5°0' W).

Alemayehu et al. 2022, Introduction + Results: inland valleys = seasonally flooded wetlands (hydromorphic fringes and valley bottoms); food provision rated the most important service; rice ranked highest crop. Regional study, not basin-wide.

Kouassi et al. 2012 §5 Discussion: runoff deficits (52%) far above rainfall deficits (16%) in the N'zi basin (figure the authors cite from Kouassi et al. 2008); break in discharge series in 1968 at Fétêkro and Dimbokro.

COL-CUM.summary: A high Andean area of Cumbal municipality in Nariño, near the Ecuador border.
COL-CUM.ecosystem: Andean highlands and páramo around the Cumbal volcano.
COL-CUM.livelihoods: Dairy cattle, potato farming and traditional 'shagra' plots with Andean tubers.
COL-CUM.why_it_matters: Its páramo supplies water, and family plots keep neglected Andean crops such as oca and mashua in use.

sources.note: Municipality in Nariño; town at ~3,172 m; Pasto indigenous homeland; resguardos
Cumbal and Chiles volcanoes; cold and páramo thermal zones
Páramo partly replaced by small family farms for dairy cattle and potato
Páramo as water source ('custodians of water')

ETH-OG.summary: Ethiopia's Omo-Gibe river basin — about 79,700 km² across four regions, running some 550 km from the south-western highlands to the Omo delta at Lake Turkana. A strong north–south gradient separates humid, densely settled highlands from semi-arid pastoral lowlands.
ETH-OG.ecosystem: Forest (31%), shrubland (29%) and grassland (20%) still cover four fifths of the basin; 23 protected and conserved sites take in about 35% of it, from the wild Arabica coffee forests of the south-west to the Omo–Tama–Mago park complex in the lower valley.
ETH-OG.livelihoods: Some 14–16 million people: coffee, enset and cereals in the densely settled highlands, maize and root crops in the crowded middle basin, and herding, flood-recession cropping and fishing in the southern lowlands.
ETH-OG.why_it_matters: It drives the Gibe hydropower cascade and supplies more than 80% of Lake Turkana's inflow, but nearly half the basin saw some deforestation between 1985 and 2020, and the regulated river no longer floods the lower Omo, where recession farming and fishing depended on it.

sources.note: Omo-Gibe landscape characterization (Tibebe et al., CGIAR/Alliance, Oct 2026) §2.1: 79,693 km²; ~550 km from the Gibe headwaters near Wenchi to the Omo delta; 34% South Ethiopia, 31% Southwest Ethiopia, 25% Oromia, 10% Central Ethiopia. Abstract: north–south gradient from humid highlands to semi-arid pastoral lowlands.

Omo-Gibe landscape characterization (Tibebe et al., CGIAR/Alliance, Oct 2026) §6.1 (ESA WorldCover 2021): forest 31.4%, shrubland 29.2%, grassland 20.0%, cropland 17.3%. §8.2: 23 sites, ~27,600 km² = 35% of the basin; Kafa Biosphere Reserve in the wild Arabica coffee forests; Omo–Tama–Mago complex ~16,500 km².

Omo-Gibe landscape characterization (Tibebe et al., CGIAR/Alliance, Oct 2026) §1.1: 13.7–16.1 million people. §7.3 (livelihood zones, FEWS NET): coffee–cereal–chat and enset–cereal zones in the north; Wolaita and Gamo–Gofa maize and root crop zones in the middle basin; South Omo pastoral and flood-recession zones in the south.

Omo-Gibe landscape characterization (Tibebe et al., CGIAR/Alliance, Oct 2026) §1.1: more than 80% of Lake Turkana's inflow; Gibe cascade ~2.5 GW installed, Koysha 2,160 MW under construction. §8.4: 48.8% of the basin with some deforestation 1985–2020; erosion hotspots on the middle-basin escarpments draining to Gibe III and Koysha. §4.4: Gibe III removed the flood pulse that supported recession farming and fishing.

resources.title: Omo-Gibe landscape characterization: an integrated biophysical and socio-economic assessment of the Omo-Gibe Landscape, Ethiopia
resources.authors: Degefie Tibebe, Getachew Tesfaye, Yonas Getaneh, Habtamu Sewnet, Meron Awoke, Kalkidan Mulatu, Kifle Woldearegay, Zenebe Adimassu, Wuletawu Abera
resources.org: Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, for the CGIAR Multifunctional Landscapes Science Programme
resources.note: Spatial baseline for the basin: climate, water, terrain and soils, land cover and land-use change, farming and livelihood systems, biodiversity and protected areas, degradation and hazards, and socio-economic conditions — with four entry points for integrated landscape management.

IND-CH.summary: Six districts of central India — Jhansi in Uttar Pradesh and Tikamgarh, Chhatarpur, Damoh, Jabalpur and Mandla in Madhya Pradesh. The first four lie in Bundelkhand, a fragile dryland with shallow, low-fertility soils, poor water retention and highly erratic rainfall.
IND-CH.ecosystem: Rainfed cropland, forests and open natural ecosystems on a hot, sub-humid upland.
IND-CH.livelihoods: In Bundelkhand, households depend heavily on rainfed farming and livestock; cropping intensity is often no more than 110%, poverty is widespread, and many people migrate to cities, leaving the elderly and children behind.
IND-CH.why_it_matters: Rainfed farms and livestock sustain rural livelihoods, but in Bundelkhand annual rainfall has fallen by nearly 250 mm over five decades, droughts are frequent, groundwater is being depleted and nearly 30% of productive farmland lies fallow in one of the two cropping seasons.

sources.note: Ecosystem Restoration through Landscape Resource Conservation: Lessons Learned from Central India (Anantha KH, Singh R, Garg KK, Venkata Radha A, Ram A, Harawa R, Jat ML; ICRISAT policy brief, October 2025) §The Context / p.2: Bundelkhand covers parts of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh; landscape 'inherently fragile' — poor water retention capacity, shallow and low-fertile soils, highly erratic rainfall. §Summary / p.1: 'dryland' Bundelkhand region of Central India. The list of six districts and which of them are Bundelkhand districts come from the landscape boundary definition, not from the brief.

Ecosystem Restoration through Landscape Resource Conservation (Anantha KH et al.; ICRISAT, 2025) §The Context / p.2: high dependency on rainfed agriculture and livestock for livelihoods; low cropping intensity, often no more than 110%; widespread distress migration to urban centres leaving elderly family members and children behind; poverty (the brief's 'over 80% below the poverty line' figure was deliberately NOT used — see problems).

Ecosystem Restoration through Landscape Resource Conservation (Anantha KH et al.; ICRISAT, 2025) §The Context / p.2: decline in annual rainfall by nearly 250 mm over the last five decades, frequent droughts; nearly 30% of Bundelkhand's productive agricultural land left fallow in either kharif or rabi season; overdependence on groundwater has led to groundwater depletion; dependence on rainfed agriculture and livestock.

KEN-LEI.summary: Four Kenyan counties near Nairobi — Kajiado, Kiambu, Machakos and Makueni. They run from Kiambu's wet, densely settled highlands on the edge of the Aberdare ranges to the semi-arid farmland of Machakos and Makueni and the pastoral rangelands of Kajiado.
KEN-LEI.ecosystem: Kiambu's main forests lie in its wet upper highlands; Makueni is half arable, with 34% shrubland and 9% grassland; on the Athi-Kapiti plains of Kajiado and Machakos, semi-arid grassland with scattered trees links Nairobi National Park to Amboseli and Tsavo.
KEN-LEI.livelihoods: Nearly six million people across the four counties (2019 census): tea, coffee, dairy and commuting to Nairobi in Kiambu; rain-fed maize, beans, pulses and fruit farming in Machakos and Makueni; and livestock herding, mainly by Maasai pastoralists, in rural Kajiado.
KEN-LEI.why_it_matters: Its plains keep wildlife moving between Nairobi National Park, Amboseli and Tsavo and Kajiado's herds supply Nairobi's meat markets, but recurrent drought and the subdivision of pastoral land for settlement — Kajiado's population grew 62.6% in ten years — are shrinking grazing land and leaving water scarce.

sources.note: Kajiado County Integrated Development Plan 2023-2027 (County Government of Kajiado, 2023) §1.1-1.2, printed p.1 / PDF p.8: area 21,872 sq km; primarily semi-arid; livestock rearing through nomadic pastoralism in rural areas. §3.4 printed p.52 / PDF p.59: most of the county in semi-arid and arid zones.

Table on PDF p.22: 952 persons per km2 in 2019 (basis for 'densely settled').

A 13,000 ha site, used only as an example of the plains.

Makueni CIDP 2023-2027 §1.5.1 p.17: 2019 census population 987,653. §1.3.3 p.14: mango and citrus, grains, cow peas, pigeon peas, green grams, sorghum by zone. p.49: reliance on rain-fed agriculture.

Supports 'shrinking grazing land'; no figure used.

KEN-LVB.summary: Five counties of western Kenya — Kericho, Kisumu, Nandi, Siaya and Vihiga — in the Lake Victoria Basin. Lowland floodplains by the lake give way to mid-altitude mixed farms and densely populated highlands; rainfall averages 1,000–1,500 mm a year.
KEN-LVB.ecosystem: A mosaic of farm fields, pastures, settlements and pockets of natural vegetation on low-organic-matter Acrisols and Cambisols, draining to Lake Victoria; Vihiga is predominantly hilly, while Kisumu's lake-adjacent lowlands flood repeatedly.
KEN-LVB.livelihoods: Smallholder households combining crops — maize, beans, cassava, sweet potatoes, bananas and vegetables — with dairy cattle, goats and poultry, informal trade and wage work; Nile perch and tilapia fisheries add food and income along the lake.
KEN-LVB.why_it_matters: Its farms and the lake's Nile perch and tilapia fisheries feed and employ a dense smallholder population, but maize yields of 2.1–2.3 t/ha in Kisumu and Vihiga sit far below the 6–8 t/ha potential, steep slopes in Vihiga erode, and farm runoff and sewage pollute the lake.

sources.note: Synthesis report on the evidence of the multifunctional performance of LVB landscape (Kaushal, Fadda, Kidane, Nyawira, Fuchs & Geck, 2025; no centre named in the front matter) §3.1 / p.4: agroecological zones from lowland floodplains near Lake Victoria to mid-altitude mixed farming systems and densely populated highland areas. §3.2 / p.4: humid equatorial climate, bimodal rainfall, average 1,000–1,500 mm annually. County list is from the MOSAIC boundary, not the report.

Same report §3.1 / p.4: land use = agricultural fields, pastures, residential areas, pockets of natural vegetation; Kisumu lake-adjacent lowlands; Vihiga predominantly hilly terrain. §3.2 / p.4: weathered Acrisols, Cambisols, low organic matter. §6 / p.9: recurrent flooding in low-lying Kisumu adjacent to the lake.

Same report §3.3 / p.7: smallholder agriculture; households rely on crop farming, livestock, informal trade, wage employment. §4 / p.7–8: maize, beans, cassava, sweet potatoes, bananas, horticultural crops (tomatoes, cabbage); dairy cattle, goats, poultry, some sheep. §3.1 / p.4: Nile perch and tilapia fisheries contribute to local diets and income.

Same report §1 / p.3: high population density, smallholder-dominated agriculture. §3.1 / p.4: fisheries for diets and income. §4 / p.7 and Table 1 / p.8: maize about 2.3 t/ha in Kisumu, 2.1 t/ha in Vihiga, potential 6–8 t/ha. §6 / p.9: significant soil erosion on Vihiga's steep hills; nutrient runoff from farms, untreated sewage and industrial effluents compromise water quality, eutrophication and algal blooms in Lake Victoria.

MEK-3S.summary: The Sekong, Sesan and Srepok river basins, Mekong tributaries shared by Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam.
MEK-3S.ecosystem: Forested uplands, rivers and floodplains, with rice fields and hydropower reservoirs.
MEK-3S.why_it_matters: About 10% of the Mekong watershed but nearly 40% of Lower Mekong fish species, and dams are changing its flows and fisheries.

sources.note: Hydropower dams in the 3S basins
3S = 10% of Mekong watershed, ~40% of LMB fish species; dams reduce fish biodiversity

PER-PCL.summary: Peru's Pucallpa–Aguaytía agroforestry corridor in the Amazonian region of Ucayali — about 14,000 km², linking the city of Pucallpa to the Aguaytía river basin. Amazon lowlands rise westward towards the Cordillera Azul and the Andean foothills, along a road frontier settled since the 1940s.
PER-PCL.ecosystem: Humid tropical rainforest — terra firme, riparian and seasonally flooded forest, with foothill forest in the west — now a mosaic of old-growth remnants, secondary forest, fallows, agro-pastoral land and agroforestry plots along the Aguaytía River, a tributary of the Ucayali.
PER-PCL.livelihoods: About 500,000 people, 81% of them urban; rural households, mestizo and Indigenous (chiefly Shipibo-Konibo), live from oil palm, rice, cacao, banana and cassava, extensive cattle, fish farming and Amazonian fruits such as camu camu.
PER-PCL.why_it_matters: Its forest mosaic stores carbon, regulates water and shelters high biodiversity while supplying cacao and oil palm to domestic and export markets, but the corridor has the highest deforestation rate in Ucayali — 40% of its forests lost in two decades to the farming frontier and infrastructure.

sources.note: Profile of MFL Ucayali, Peru (Arce, A.; International Potato Center (CIP), 2026) §1 / PDF p.5: corridor nested in Ucayali region, links Pucallpa (Coronel Portillo) to Aguaytía river basin (Padre Abad), area 14,064.11 km²; §3 / p.6: ~1.4 million ha (14,064 km²), ~14% of Ucayali; §5 / p.7: Amazon lowlands and Amazon-Andean transition, relief increasing westward, runoff from Cordillera Azul and Andean foothills; §4 / p.6: road-frontier history, Federico Basadre highway from the 1940s, Andean migration.

Profile of MFL Ucayali, Peru (Arce, A.; CIP, 2026) §5 / PDF p.7: humid tropical rainforest, terra firme, riparian and seasonally flooded forests, foothill forest to the west; Aguaytía River a major tributary of the Ucayali crossing the corridor; §3 / p.6: mosaic of old-growth remnants, secondary forests, fallows, agro-pastoral systems, agroforestry plots. No land-cover percentages are given in the report.

Profile of MFL Ucayali, Peru (Arce, A.; CIP, 2026) §9 / PDF p.8: estimated population of the landscape 500,466 (INEI 2020), 81% urban; §10 / p.9: mestizo majority, Shipibo-Konibo the principal Indigenous group in both provinces; §15 / pp.11-12: Table 1 crops for Padre Abad and Coronel Portillo (oil palm, rice, cacao, banana, cassava — names only, figures not used), extensive cattle, aquaculture (paco, gamitana, paiche), camu camu and other Amazonian fruits.

Profile of MFL Ucayali, Peru (Arce, A.; CIP, 2026) §2 / PDF p.5: corridor has the highest deforestation rate in Ucayali over the last two decades, 40% of its forests lost to agricultural-frontier expansion and infrastructure; §6 / p.7: ecosystem mosaic underpins high biodiversity, carbon storage, water regulation; §16 / p.12: cacao and oil palm are the most consolidated value chains linking the corridor to domestic and international markets.

SEN-FK.summary: Fatick Department in west-central Senegal lies between the inland farming and grazing zones and the Sine-Saloum estuary, reaching the Atlantic to the west. It is a Sudano-Sahelian area with 500–700 mm of rain a year, highly variable from one year to the next.
SEN-FK.ecosystem: A mosaic of rainfed cropland, extensive grazing land, forest resources and wetlands on mainly tropical ferruginous soils, with salt-affected land in the south and near the coast; in Niakhar commune, cropland averaged 19,581 ha over 2016–2025.
SEN-FK.livelihoods: Rainfed farming and extensive livestock keeping are the main livelihoods; in Niakhar commune farmers grow groundnut, millet, sorghum and cowpea, herds graze the harvested fields in the dry season, and women and young people run small market gardens.
SEN-FK.why_it_matters: Its cropland, grazing land, forest resources and wetlands support farming and herding side by side, but soil degradation, salinization, scarcer woody biomass and growing pressure on land, sharpened by variable rainfall, are lowering yields and fuelling conflicts between farmers and herders.

sources.note: Stakeholder platforms and governance of multifunctional landscapes in the department of Fatick (Mané & Tounkara, ISRA; Piraux, CIRAD, 2026) §3.1.2–3.1.3 / p.11 (printed p.10): department in central-western Senegal; pivot between continental agro-sylvo-pastoral zones and Sine-Saloum estuarine zones; bordered W by the Atlantic; Sudano-Sahelian zone; average annual rainfall 500–700 mm; high interannual variability

Stakeholder platforms and governance of multifunctional landscapes in the department of Fatick (Mané & Tounkara, ISRA; Piraux, CIRAD, 2026) §3.1.3 / p.11–12: soils mainly tropical ferruginous; salinization in southern and coastal parts; landscapes interlink rain-fed agriculture, extensive livestock, forest resources and wetlands

Analysis of the Niakhar landscape using satellite imagery (M. Dieye, O. Dieye & M. Piraux, 2026; no centre stated in front matter) §3.1.1 / p.11 and Table 2 / p.15: Niakhar municipality cultivated area averages 19,581 ha over 2016–2025 (range 14,583–23,070 ha)

Stakeholder platforms and governance of multifunctional landscapes in the department of Fatick (Mané & Tounkara, ISRA; Piraux, CIRAD, 2026) §3.1.3 / p.12 and §4.1 / p.15: agro-sylvo-pastoral production systems; rain-fed agriculture and extensive livestock farming

Analysis of the Niakhar landscape using satellite imagery (M. Dieye, O. Dieye & M. Piraux, 2026; no centre stated in front matter) Table 1 / p.10: crops = peanuts, millet, sorghum, cowpeas; §4.5 / p.17–18: harvested plots grazed in the dry season; small market gardens mainly worked by women and young people (Niakhar only)

Stakeholder platforms and governance of multifunctional landscapes in the department of Fatick (Mané & Tounkara, ISRA; Piraux, CIRAD, 2026) §3.1.3 / p.12: multifunctional interconnection of agriculture, livestock, forest resources, wetlands; §4.1 / p.15: soil degradation, salinization, increasing scarcity of woody biomass, pressure on agricultural and pastoral land, climate variability, declining yields, recurring farmer–herder conflicts

TUN-NW.summary: Seven rural sectors of Le Kef and Siliana governorates in semi-arid northwestern Tunisia.
TUN-NW.ecosystem: Rainfed cereal land, olive groves, rangeland and forest patches on erosion-prone hills.
TUN-NW.livelihoods: Small mixed farms: cereals, olives and sheep and goats.
TUN-NW.why_it_matters: Its hills carry cereals, olives and grazing for small farms, but water erosion is stripping their thin soils.

sources.note: Olive and rainfed cereals; erosion
El Kef-Siliana: semi-arid, mixed cereal–tree–small ruminant systems
Water erosion as main degradation

ZWE-MB.summary: Four districts of Zimbabwe's Zambezi Valley — Mbire, Muzarabani, Mount Darwin and Hurungwe. Mbire district, about 250 km north of Harare on the Zambia and Mozambique borders, is a semi-arid wildlife–agriculture mosaic of about 4,700 km² with 83,724 residents (2022 census).
ZWE-MB.ecosystem: In Mbire district, forest and woodland — mopane, miombo, Combretum–Terminalia and acacia — cover around 70%, with scrub, open grassland, riverine forest and wetlands; in Ward 2, mapped cropland is only 5–6% within a shrub, forest and grass matrix.
ZWE-MB.livelihoods: About 80% of Mbire district's households depend on crop production — rainfed maize, sorghum, cotton, sesame and groundnuts on plots typically under 1.5 ha — alongside goats, poultry and cattle, casual labour, fishing and wild foods.
ZWE-MB.why_it_matters: Mbire district's woodlands, rivers and floodplains sustain wildlife, flood-recession farming and non-timber products between major conservation areas, but drought is chronic, floods recur almost yearly and elephants and baboons raid crops; about 55% of rural households were estimated cereal insecure at the January–March 2025 hunger peak.

sources.note: Synthesis report on the multifunctional performance of Mbire landscape (Falconnier, Sibanda & Chimonyo, 2025; CGIAR, no centre named in front matter) §Description and context, p.5: semi-arid wildlife–agriculture mosaic; Mashonaland Central; approx. 250 km north of Harare; close to Zambia and Mozambique borders (Luangwa District N, Tete Province NE, Muzarabani E, Hurungwe W); district area 4,695.87 km²; 2022 census 83,724 residents; p.8: mid-Zambezi valley.
